name: Gareth Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can be as honest as you like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No problem at all. I'm the shop steward at work, so I'm used to people asking what I really think. Usually it's the boss, though.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead electrician at Brennock Building Services in Hollin Bridge. We do commercial work, shop fit-outs, the primary school, the leisure centre, the odd unit on the trading estate. Right now I've got three lads fitting out a new pharmacy on Station Road: lighting, sockets, fire alarm, the lot. I plan the day at seven, I'm on the tools by eight, and I do the risk assessments and the test sheets at the end.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a fit-out coming together, when the lights go on in an empty shell and it suddenly looks like a shop. What wears me out is the paperwork, and being paid less than the job's worth. Brennock pays under the going rate because there's hardly anyone else round here hiring, and they know it. I've still got about nine hundred on a credit card from when Ana and I moved in together, and less than a month of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. Half the lads were convinced robots would be pulling cable by next year. I'd say it in the canteen and probably on the five-a-side group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the same squeeze as now. My pay doesn't move unless the union moves it, and the rent goes up anyway. The bit of AI that sticks around is the stuff I already use now and then, like getting a draft risk assessment written quickly, and that's handy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off that nine hundred on the card by the summer, a hundred and fifty a month. I'd keep pushing for the regional rate at the next pay talks. And I'd keep using the AI for the boring paperwork where it's proven it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with the usual low hum about money. The robots aren't what I lose sleep over. The credit card statement is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the usual low hum about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's that one bad month would sink us. If the van broke and I had to use my own car for a fortnight, or Ana's hours got cut, we'd be straight onto the card again. There's no slack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use the AI now, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe twice a week. I tell it the job, say a consumer unit swap in a school kitchen, and it gives me a first go at the risk assessment. I check every line, because it once told me to isolate a circuit that doesn't exist.

say: The robot talk was **overblown**, and the lads who feared it were wrong.
The **pay squeeze** is the real story in the trade, not AI.
think: Nothing changes, so his **pay only moves** when the union moves it.
The AI he uses for **risk assessments** is handy, but needs checking.
do: Pay off the **£900 credit card** at £150 a month by summer.
Push for the **regional rate** at the next pay talks.
Keep using AI for **draft paperwork**, checking every line.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with a low hum of money worry about one bad month.
S0.quote: The robots aren't what I lose sleep over. The credit card statement is.
fieldNote: His real pressure is a **£900 card balance** and no slack for one bad month.
He's a **careful user** of AI: twice a week, checking every line after it invented a circuit.
As **shop steward** he frames everything through pay talks.

steps.text: Pay £150 a month off the credit card until it's clear
Push for the regional pay rate at Brennock's next talks
Keep drafting school risk assessments with AI, then check them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift and we need to get ahead of it as a union, not wait for it. Electricians are fine for now, but the people in offices aren't. I'd say that at the branch, and I'd say it to Brennock's managers too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my own job's safe for a good few years. My work is in ceilings and risers, not on a screen. The worry is my partner Ana, who answers tenants and books repairs at the council. She does the admin at the housing office, and that's exactly the list on your card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools properly for the planning side, because the other firms will, and I'd want Brennock to win the tenders. I'd get the union to ask for a training budget for the office staff. And Ana and I would sit down and look at what she could retrain into, maybe something in housing that's face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for me, worried for us. That's the honest split.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, and we're a team, and she's not going to be the one left holding it. She'd say I always say that. She'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your money if Ana's job goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be on my wage alone, which covers rent and not much else. The card would come back, and we'd have to stop the plan to save for a deposit, which is barely started anyway.

say: The union must **get ahead** of this rather than wait for it.
Electricians are fine for now, but **office workers** aren't.
think: His own work in ceilings and risers is **safe for years**.
His partner **Ana's job**, answering tenants and booking repairs, is exactly what AI takes.
do: Learn the **AI planning tools** properly so Brennock wins tenders.
Ask the union for a **training budget** for office staff.
Sit down with Ana to plan a **face-to-face retrain** in housing.
feel: **Uneasy** for himself and **worried** for the household.
S1.quote: My work is in ceilings and risers, not on a screen. The worry is my partner Ana, who answers tenants and books repairs at the council.
fieldNote: The household risk sits with **Ana's council admin job**, not his own.

steps.text: Learn the AI tender and planning tools Brennock's rivals use
Ask the union branch for an office staff training budget
Help Ana find a face-to-face housing course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it publicly: this is a crisis and it needs a crisis response, like a pandemic. Income support, paid retraining, and the companies making the money paying for it. I'd be organising, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Ana's job goes almost at once, and mine follows around 2031. Two years isn't time for anything. With the thinking AI here, Brennock's office could shrink to one person, and then I'd be working on borrowed time until the robots can climb a ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away, the streaming, the takeaways, my five-a-side subs. I'd go to my parents and ask whether we could move into their back bedroom in Lowfield to save the rent if Ana's pay stops. And I'd be at every union meeting and lobbying the council and the MP for a jobs guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared. I'm meant to be the steady one, and I wouldn't feel steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be on borrowed time until the robots come. What would you do in those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work every hour Brennock gives me and save the lot. And I'd be looking at what a person still has to do when robots wire buildings. Someone has to sign off, someone has to fix the robot. I'd want to be that person, but I wouldn't know how in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents take that conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say yes before I'd finished. My dad would say yes too, but he'd want me to help with his allotment shed. Honestly, that's the part that would sting, being twenty-nine and back in my old room.

say: This is a **crisis** and needs a pandemic-style response.
The firms making money must **pay for retraining** and income support.
think: Ana's job **goes almost at once**, and his follows around 2031.
He'd be **on borrowed time** until robots can climb a ladder.
do: Cut **streaming, takeaways** and five-a-side subs straight away.
Ask his parents about moving into their **back bedroom** in Lowfield.
Lobby the council and MP for a **jobs guarantee**.
feel: **Properly scared**, and unsettled that the steady one wouldn't feel steady.
S2.quote: I'm meant to be the steady one, and I wouldn't feel steady.
fieldNote: He expects both **household incomes** to go within five years.
He'd use the three-year **robot gap** to save and look for robot maintenance or sign-off work.
Moving back home at **twenty-nine** would sting more than the money.

steps.text: Cancel streaming, takeaways and five-a-side subs
Ask his parents to move into their back bedroom in Lowfield
Lobby the council and MP for a jobs guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for not planning. I'd want the union and the colleges sitting down together now, not in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to change direction once. The thinking AI lands in 2031, then robots for hands-on work around 2034. That gives me seven-odd years on the tools, and time to pick something robots won't do first, like big battery systems and grid connections where you need a licence and judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the battery storage and EV charging course at the college in Morley next September, evenings, about four hundred quid I'd have to save for. I'd clear the card first. And I'd help Ana pick her retraining in the first two years, while her office still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but with a plan. Five years is enough that I feel like I'm doing something, not just waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why battery systems and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every building's going to want one, and the grid people need a licensed person on the connection. I've done two for Brennock already. A robot might fit the battery box, but someone's still answerable for the grid connection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd clear the card first. Is that realistic on your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just about, if nothing breaks. It's six months of a hundred and fifty. Then I start saving for the course. It's tight, but it's a plan I can see.

Help Ana choose her **retraining** within two years.
feel: **Nervous**, but steadied by having a plan he can see.
S3.quote: A robot might fit the battery box, but someone's still answerable for the grid connection.
fieldNote: He maps **2031 and 2034** onto his own career and counts seven years on the tools.

The plan depends on **nothing breaking** for six months of card payments.

steps.text: Clear the £900 card at £150 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and the government had better not waste it. A decade is enough to retrain a whole workforce if anyone bothers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels manageable for me. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking AI arrives and forty when the robots do. By then I want to be the one installing and fixing the robots and batteries, not competing with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the battery course, then the robotics maintenance one when it exists, and I'd use the AI tools every day by then like everyone else. I'd still keep my union card. And Ana and I would finally plan the wedding and save for a deposit, because ten years means we can't just freeze our lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. There's still a knot about Ana, and about money, but it feels like a race I could actually run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the wedding come up here and not in the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in the fast ones every penny's for survival. With ten years, I'm not putting my life with my partner on hold for a robot. We'd marry small, at her nan's church hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still keeps the knot there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana's job still goes in the end. Ten years just means it goes slower. And I've got no savings to speak of, so any plan of mine is one bad year from falling apart.

A decade is enough to **retrain a workforce** if anyone bothers.

He wants to be the one **fixing robots and batteries**, not competing with them.

Use **AI tools daily** for planning and paperwork.

feel: **Mostly hopeful**, with a knot about Ana's job and the thin cushion.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Both of us out of work inside five years, and no cushion. What would help is paid retraining that actually pays a wage while you do it, so people like me and Ana can afford to go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the apprentices. If firms stop taking on apprentices because robots are coming, there won't be anyone to check the robots' work in ten years. Somebody needs to keep training sparkies, and that's a choice, not a law of nature.

headlineQuote: If firms stop taking on apprentices because robots are coming, there won't be anyone to check the robots' work in ten years.
portrait: Gareth is a 27-year-old **lead electrician** and shop steward doing commercial fit-outs in Hollin Bridge.
He carries a **£900 card balance** and under a month of savings, on below-rate pay.
He uses AI **now and then** for risk assessments and would learn more once rivals prove it.
His biggest exposure is his partner **Ana's council admin job**, which drives his mood from Steady Disruption on.
With time, he'd retrain into **battery and robot maintenance** and stop freezing his personal plans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both household jobs gone inside five years and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** that covers a wage while you study.
Firms keeping on **apprentices** so people remain to check robot work.
